sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A small office/home office network needs correct IP configuration before devices can communicate reliably.
For this objective, recognize IPv4, private and public addressing, IPv6, APIPA, static and dynamic assignment, subnet masks, and default gateways.
sections.callout: ADDRESS → MASK → GATEWAY.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a SOHO device cannot communicate, can you determine whether its IP address, address type, subnet mask, or gateway is responsible?

sections.title: Internet Protocol (IP) Addressing
paragraphs: An IP address identifies a device logically on an IP network. Devices require compatible IP configuration to communicate, and the two major versions are IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.callout: IP address = logical network address.

sections.title: IPv4
paragraphs: Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) uses 32-bit addresses written as four decimal octets separated by periods. Each octet ranges from 0 through 255.
sections.callout: 192.168.1.10 and other four-part dotted-decimal addresses → IPv4.

sections.title: Private IPv4 Addresses
paragraphs: Private IPv4 addresses are used inside private networks and are not directly routed across the public internet. Separate homes and organizations can reuse the same private ranges.

sections.title: Public IPv4 Addresses
paragraphs: A public IPv4 address is globally routable on the public internet. In many SOHO networks, internal devices use private addresses while the internet-facing connection receives a public address from the provider.
sections.callout: Address used directly on the public internet → public IPv4.

sections.title: Private vs. Public IPv4

table.caption: IPv4 address visibility
rows: Used internally and not directly routed across the public internet

sections.callout: Private stays inside; public faces outside.

sections.title: IPv6
paragraphs: Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) uses 128-bit addresses written with hexadecimal groups separated by colons. Its much larger address space addresses IPv4 scarcity.
sections.callout: 2001:db8::10 and other colon-separated hexadecimal addresses → IPv6.

sections.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6
sections.callout: Dots and decimal → IPv4; colons and hexadecimal → IPv6.

sections.title: Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA)
paragraphs: Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA) lets an IPv4 device assign itself an address when it cannot obtain normal configuration from DHCP. APIPA uses 169.254.0.0/16.
sections.callout: 169.254.x.x → APIPA → DHCP did not answer.

sections.title: What APIPA Usually Means
paragraphs: On a SOHO network that normally uses DHCP, APIPA indicates that the client expected automatic addressing but failed to receive it. Possible causes include DHCP failure, bad cabling, wireless problems, a switch issue, or router trouble.
sections.callout: Treat 169.254 as a troubleshooting clue, not an ordinary static address.

sections.title: APIPA Limitations
paragraphs: APIPA can permit limited communication between devices on the same local APIPA network, but it normally does not provide proper access to other networks or the internet because the client lacks normal configuration such as a gateway.
sections.callout: APIPA = local survival mode, not normal network configuration.

sections.title: Static Addressing
paragraphs: A static IP address is manually configured and remains assigned until changed. It suits servers, printers, network appliances, and infrastructure devices that need predictable addresses.
sections.callout: Manually configured predictable address → static.

sections.title: Dynamic Addressing
paragraphs: A dynamic IP address is assigned automatically, commonly by DHCP, and may change over time. It is convenient for laptops, phones, tablets, and workstations.
sections.callout: Client automatically receives settings → dynamic.

sections.title: Static vs. Dynamic
sections.callout: Static = fixed manually; dynamic = automatic.

sections.title: Static Address vs. DHCP Reservation

table.caption: Two ways to provide a predictable address
rows: On the DHCP server; the endpoint still uses DHCP

sections.callout: Static = device decides; reservation = DHCP decides.

sections.title: Subnet Mask
paragraphs: A subnet mask tells an IPv4 host which part of an address identifies the network and which part identifies the host. The device uses it to decide whether a destination is local or must be sent toward a gateway.
sections.callout: Subnet mask = who is local?

sections.title: Common SOHO Subnet Mask
paragraphs: A common SOHO mask is 255.255.255.0, which corresponds to /24. With that mask, the first three octets identify the network portion.

sections.title: How the Subnet Mask Decides
paragraphs: With a /24 mask, 192.168.1.20 and 192.168.1.50 are local to one another, while 192.168.2.50 is on a different network and must be reached through a gateway.
sections.callout: The mask decides local versus remote.

sections.title: Default Gateway
paragraphs: The default gateway is the device address a host uses when a destination is outside the local network. In a SOHO network, it is commonly the router's local IP address.
sections.callout: Local communication works but remote networks fail → check the default gateway.

sections.title: Gateway vs. Router

table.caption: Exit device and exit address
rows: The IP address a client uses as its exit path

sections.callout: Router = box; gateway = address of the exit.

sections.title: IP Address vs. Subnet Mask vs. Gateway

table.caption: Three essential host settings
rows: How do I leave this network?

sections.callout: ADDRESS → MASK → GATEWAY.

sections.title: SOHO IPv4 Configuration Example
paragraphs: On network 192.168.10.0/24, a laptop could use address 192.168.10.25, mask 255.255.255.0, and gateway 192.168.10.1. The address identifies the laptop, the mask identifies local destinations, and the gateway receives remote traffic.

sections.title: Recognizing a Misconfigured Address
paragraphs: If a device should be on 192.168.1.0/24 but is configured as 192.168.2.40 with a /24 mask, it belongs to a different logical subnet. A connected cable does not guarantee valid IP connectivity.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Path to outside networks → default gateway

sections.title: Objective 2.6 Exam Trap
paragraphs: IP address, subnet mask, and gateway appear together but are not interchangeable. Match the symptom to the setting's job.

entries.title: Private vs. Public IPv4
paragraphs: Only 172.16 through 172.31 belongs to the private 172 block; 10/8 and 192.168/16 are the other private ranges.

entries.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6
paragraphs: Dotted decimal points to IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal points to IPv6.

entries.title: APIPA vs. Normal Private Address
paragraphs: 192.168.x.x is commonly intentional private addressing; 169.254.x.x is self-assignment after automatic IPv4 configuration fails.

entries.title: Static vs. Dynamic
paragraphs: Typed manually means static; automatically obtained means dynamic. A DHCP reservation can make a dynamic address predictable.

entries.title: Subnet Mask vs. Gateway
paragraphs: The mask decides which destinations are local; the gateway provides the path to destinations that are not local.

entries.title: Local vs. Internet Connectivity
paragraphs: If local communication works but remote networks fail and addressing is valid, inspect the gateway. If the client has 169.254.x.x, investigate DHCP or connectivity first.

sections.callout: Mask decides; gateway exits.
